# Signet Artists

> Signet Artists delivers live entertainment for private events in Denver, Colorado and surrounding areas. All provided in a variety of genres and configurations - effortlessly.

Signet Artists is a live music company for private events in Denver, Boulder, and the mountain corridor. No prices are published. What the pricing page carries is what live music costs in the Colorado market, each price with the source it came from, and Signet prices a specific night when the date is sent.

## Credits

Trusted and booked by Amazon, NBCUniversal, Charles Schwab, Kroger, Denver Art Museum, Sheraton, Hyatt, Gaylord Rockies Resort & Convention Center, Washington Nationals, Casa Bonita and Monarch Casino Resort Spa Black Hawk. Plus Live Nation, the stages at Dazzle, the Bluebird Theater, Cervantes, and many, many more.

## Blog

- [Chelsey Webb joins Signet Artists](https://signetartists.com/blog/chelsey-webb-joins-signet-artists/): This post announces that Chelsey Webb, a Denver country singer raised in Alabama and named Female Entertainer of the Year at the 2025 Colorado Country Music Hall of Fame awards, is now a Featured Artist with Signet Artists. It covers the stages she has played, the covers and original songs she performs, and how to book her as a duo or with her five or six-piece band for weddings, parties and corporate events in Colorado.
- [Why guests can't hear the toast](https://signetartists.com/blog/why-guests-cant-hear-the-toast/): A plain-language guide for event planners on speech clarity at weddings and corporate events: why toasts and announcements get lost (microphone held at the chest, feedback squeal when the speaker walks toward a loudspeaker, background music left up), how much louder than the background a voice needs to be (about 10 to 15 decibels; older listeners need a few more), what the band's sound person does before guests arrive (ringing out the microphone), and three questions to ask: who controls the volume during speeches, is a second microphone switched on, and will the microphone be tested from the spot where the toasts happen.
- [Why dinner gets louder as the night goes on](https://signetartists.com/blog/why-dinner-gets-louder/): A plain-language explanation for event planners of why dinners and receptions get louder over the evening: once background sound passes roughly 57 decibels, guests raise their voices (the Lombard effect), which raises the background, which raises every voice again. It summarizes field research on what loud music does to guests (faster, heavier drinking at 88 dB vs 72 dB; about 20% more unhealthy orders at 70 dB vs 55 dB; food tasting less sweet and salty in loud noise; older adults needing more signal over noise), notes that noise was the top complaint in Zagat's 2018 survey, and describes the fix: one agreed level for dinner that sits under conversation, a second level once the dance floor opens.
- [What your venue does to the sound](https://signetartists.com/blog/what-your-venue-does-to-the-sound/): A plain-language guide for event planners on how a venue's materials and shape change the sound of a live band: low notes pass through walls (the complaint from the event next door) while the crisp parts of speech and music are absorbed by soft surfaces and by people, so an empty-venue sound check misleads; glass, marble and concrete reflect the high end and feel harsh, carpet and drapes absorb it and leave the low end booming; reverberation (how long sound hangs after it stops) blurs speech, with a clap test to judge it; and speaker placement: aim at people rather than walls, and halving the distance to a listener adds about 6 decibels, so a second small pair of speakers halfway down a long hall covers the back better than a bigger pair at the front. Ends with what to tell the band about the venue.
- [Meghan Clarisse joins Signet Artists](https://signetartists.com/blog/meghan-clarisse-joins-signet-artists/): This post announces that Meghan Clarisse, an award-winning Denver country and Americana singer-songwriter, is now a Featured Artist with Signet Artists. It covers her awards, including the 2026 Josie Music Award for Folk/Americana Album of the Year for Shadows of a Ghost Town, and how to book her solo, as a duo or with her five-piece band for weddings, parties and corporate events in Colorado.
- [How much sound system does an event need?](https://signetartists.com/blog/how-much-sound-system-does-an-event-need/): A plain-language guide for event planners on sizing a band's sound system: doubling amplifier power adds only about 3 decibels and sounding twice as loud takes roughly ten times the power, so wattage is a weak guide; headroom (spare capacity) is what keeps sound clean, because a speaker near its limit distorts and distortion is what people hear as loud; speaker count and placement cover a hall more evenly than size. It also explains event power: a standard 15-amp circuit gives about 1,800 watts and a 20-amp circuit about 2,400, a coffee urn alone draws 1,000 to 1,500 watts, outlets along a wall often share a circuit with catering, and powered speakers on a shared circuit trip the breaker. Ask the venue for a dedicated 20-amp circuit near the band, ideally two.
- [Why does music bring back memories?](https://signetartists.com/blog/why-does-music-bring-back-memories/): Signet Artists, a Denver live-music booking company, put together this research summary on why music brings back memories. A 2021 study of 657 adults representative of the British population found memories brought back by music were relived more strongly, felt more personally important and involved other people more than memories brought back by television shows, even when the songs and shows were equally familiar. A 2016 University of Iowa lab study found songs brought back memories with more detail of a particular time and place than photographs of famous faces did, and a 2021 diary study of 31 people found music brought back about one memory a day, usually during routine activities and without any effort. In a 2007 study about 30% of chart songs from college students' childhood and teens brought back a memory, mostly with positive feelings and often nostalgia, and a 2020 study of 470 people aged 18 to 82 found the songs bringing back the most memories came from people's teens, peaking around age 14. A 2024 study of 582 American adults found nostalgic songs felt more positive and energizing than songs that were only familiar, though people who tend toward sadness felt worse with them. A 2020 Australian survey of 200 people in relationships found it common for a couple to have a song they call theirs, usually picked up early in the relationship. The post closes with how to use a couple's or a guest of honor's own songs at an anniversary or milestone party.
- [Why do restaurants have live music?](https://signetartists.com/blog/why-do-restaurants-have-live-music/): This research summary comes from a Denver live-music booking company, and it's written for the owner or manager of a restaurant, hotel bar or lounge who's deciding whether a regular night of live music is worth it. In a 2024 field experiment across 282 tables at an Italian restaurant in Tel Aviv, tables stayed about 80 minutes with slow music, about 69 with the restaurant's usual playlist and about 57 with fast music, and the size of the check did not change. A 1986 study in one American restaurant found the same about time and reported more bar spending with slow music, which the 2024 experiment did not find. A 2002 study in Glasgow found that how much diners liked the music predicted their stay better than its tempo, and that time at the table best predicted spending. In a 2022 study of 248 people in a Finnish cafeteria, meals lasted longer with any sound than in silence. Two 2003 studies, each in one restaurant, linked classical music with more spending per head in Britain, and jazz, pop or classical with a higher stated willingness to pay in Sydney. A 2003 California study found larger checks with soft music than loud, and acoustics research recommends background music at no more than 60 to 65 decibels, a level two people can talk across. A 2018 study of a public square in Harbin, China, found people walked more slowly near music and sat closer to it, and a 2019 study found an audience moved more at a live show than to the same album played back. The company found no study comparing live with recorded music on a restaurant's or bar's sales. The company books solo musicians and duos for restaurants, hotel bars and lounges, for one night or a standing night.
- [Why do people sing along?](https://signetartists.com/blog/why-do-people-sing-along/): A Denver live-music booking company wrote this research summary on why people sing along at concerts and parties. In a 2012 field study, researchers counted how many people sang along to 1,054 songs over 30 nights in five venues in the north of England, some with DJs and some with live bands. The setting explained about 40% of the difference between songs, with people singing more later in the night, on weekends, in bigger venues, in younger crowds and to songs that had spent four weeks or more in the charts. The way a song was sung explained about another 25%, with people joining in more on a full chest voice, a lot of vocal effort, clear consonants and few long runs of notes on one syllable. One observer did the counting. A 2011 brain-imaging study found that dopamine is released while a listener anticipates a favorite moment in a song. A 2015 British study of 135 adults found that people in new singing classes felt closer to their classmates after the first month than people in craft or creative-writing classes, who caught up by the third month, and a 2016 study of a London community choir found the jump in closeness after 90 minutes of singing was bigger in a choir of 232 than in groups of 20 to 80. The post closes with how to choose songs for a party and two acts built around singing along, live band karaoke and a Beatles sing-along.
- [Why do people play music at funerals?](https://signetartists.com/blog/why-do-people-play-music-at-funerals/): This is a summary of what research says about music at funerals, from a Denver company that books musicians for funerals and memorial services. A study of funerals in Scotland found music used in five ways: to give the service a shape, to bring people in or leave them out, to give everyone something to do together, to stir or shift feeling, and to bring the person who died to mind, and noted that the music has moved from mostly sacred to often secular as funerals have become more personal. A 2020 Dutch study of personalized funerals found families choose a song for its connection to the person, and that what it meant in their life matters more than its words; the researcher called it a musical eulogy. In a 2022 Swedish study of 12 people who had arranged a farewell, choosing the music together gave mourners something active to do, and those who chose it in advance with the relative who was dying described that as a comfort. In a 2013 Australian study of eight bereaved caregivers, music helped them feel still connected to the person, and some stayed away from particular songs for a while. A 2024 Dutch study found funeral songs less upbeat, lower in energy and more often acoustic than other songs, and a large British funeral company's 2025 most-requested list, reported by STV News, included Time to Say Goodbye, My Way, Somewhere Over the Rainbow, You'll Never Walk Alone and Abide With Me, the only hymn in its top ten. The research is interviews and studies of what gets played; no trial of music at a funeral was found. There isn't a right answer. The song that was theirs is usually the one, and it can be a hymn or not.
- [Why do dementia patients remember music?](https://signetartists.com/blog/why-do-dementia-patients-remember-music/): This is a research summary from a Denver live-music booking company on why people living with dementia often remember songs. A 2015 study mapped the two brain areas most involved in recognizing long-known songs in 32 healthy young adults, then found those areas had shrunk less and kept using energy more normally than most of the brain in 20 people with Alzheimer's disease; the authors say this may explain what families see, though the areas were mapped in young people and memory was not tested. A small 2012 French study found that people with probable Alzheimer's disease recalled life events more specifically, faster and with more feeling after hearing music they had chosen than in silence. A 2015 review by two researchers said the popular picture of music as untouched in the brain goes further than the evidence, that careful studies were very scarce, that different dementias affect different kinds of musical memory, and that music still brings back memories and feelings and gives caregivers a way to connect without words. The 2025 Cochrane review (30 trials, 1,720 people) found no clear effect of music programs on thinking and memory. A 2015 study of 73 people with dementia found about half had changed in how they responded to sound. A 2024 study of 112 healthy older adults found the songs that felt most personal were released when the listener was about 10 to 30. Remembering a song isn't a treatment.
- [What music do 80 year olds listen to?](https://signetartists.com/blog/what-music-do-80-year-olds-listen-to/): This is a research summary from a Denver live-music booking company for anyone choosing music for an older person or a group of older adults. A 2020 study of 470 people aged 18 to 82 found the songs bringing back the most memories came from each person's teens, peaking around age 14 inside a span of roughly ages 10 to 30, and a 2025 study of 1,891 people in many countries put the peak for personally meaningful songs at 17. From those two studies the company worked out the years each age was 10 to 30 as of 2026: 1961 to 1981 for a 75-year-old, 1956 to 1976 for an 80-year-old, 1951 to 1971 for 85, 1946 to 1966 for 90 and 1941 to 1961 for 95. Someone who is 80 in 2026 was 17 or 18 when the Beatles first played The Ed Sullivan Show in February 1964, and big band was their parents' music. A 2013 Cornell study of 62 college students found a second peak for the music of their parents' youth. A 2017 study of people born from 1940 to 1999 found the pull of the late teens and early twenties was stronger in older listeners and that the oldest listeners liked the widest range of years. A 2015 German study of 48 adults with an average age of 67 found songs from across five decades of their lives still brought back memories. These are averages, and the surest way to know is to ask the person or their family.
- [Sing-along songs for seniors](https://signetartists.com/blog/sing-along-songs-for-seniors/): A list of sing-along songs for older adults from a Denver live-music booking company, with the research on choosing songs and on group singing. The songs are grouped as standards, the Beatles, Motown and soul, the sixties and seventies, and country and folk, all from the company's own song list. A 2024 study of 112 older adults found the songs that felt most personal were released when the listener was about 10 to 30, and a 2025 study of 1,891 people put the peak at 17; by the company's arithmetic that is roughly 1956 to 1976 for a resident who is 80 in 2026 and 1946 to 1966 for one who is 90. A study of 1,054 songs across 30 nights in five venues in the north of England found people sang along more to songs sung in a full voice with clear words. In a San Francisco trial of 390 people in 12 senior centers, six months of weekly choir lowered loneliness and raised interest in life more than waiting did, with no change in thinking and memory, physical strength or depression. In an English trial of 258 people aged 60 and over, community singers scored a little better on mental wellbeing at six months, with bigger gains at three months that partly faded. A 2015 British study of 135 adults found singing classes felt closer to each other after a month than craft and writing classes, which caught up by the third month. All three studied weekly group singing, and none was done in memory care.
- [Last song of the night at a wedding](https://signetartists.com/blog/last-song-of-the-night-wedding/): This is a research summary from Signet Artists, a Denver live-music booking company, on why the last song of the night at a wedding reception matters. In a 1996 study of 154 colonoscopy patients and 133 kidney-stone patients, how people remembered the procedure followed its worst moment and its last three minutes, and its length made no difference. A 2022 review that combined 174 results found the high point and the ending together predicted how people remembered an experience about as well as its overall average did, for good experiences too, and length had almost no effect. A small 2004 lab study found the same pattern for pieces of music. On the other side, a 2014 study of 54 students who each heard 11 whole songs found the average feeling all the way through predicted memory slightly better than the high point and the ending. A 2008 study of 49 students found the length of a vacation of about a week had no effect on how they remembered it, and a 2012 field study of 1,054 songs across 30 nights in five venues in the north of England found people sang along more to songs played later in the night. None of the studies took place at a wedding. The post closes with how couples choose between one more sing-along and a slow last dance.
- [Karaoke team building](https://signetartists.com/blog/karaoke-team-building/): A research summary from a Denver live-music booking company for anyone weighing karaoke for a team offsite or a company evening. The company found no study of karaoke at a company event. In a 2015 British study of 135 adults, people in new singing classes felt closer to their classmates after the first month than people in craft or creative-writing classes, who caught up by the third month; people chose their own classes. In a 2016 study of a London community choir, people felt more connected after 90 minutes of singing in groups of 20 to 80 and in one choir of 232, with a bigger jump in the large choir, where most people didn't know each other. A 2006 study found music was the topic strangers talked about most when asked to get to know each other. In a 2016 Oxford study of 94 people dancing in groups of four, the groups that danced in time said they felt closer but did no better on a cooperation game, and a 2022 paper by three music researchers warned that most studies of doing things in time together don't guard against the experimenters' expectations and that several effects were not found again when repeated with more safeguards. The post concludes that singing together seems to help people feel closer quickly but hasn't been shown to make a team cooperate better, and describes live band karaoke, where a guest sings with a live band instead of a backing track.
- [Does music make food taste better?](https://signetartists.com/blog/does-music-make-food-taste-better/): A research summary from Signet Artists, a Denver live-music booking company, on whether music changes how food and wine taste. A 2019 review by researchers at Oxford and elsewhere reported that people who like the music tend to like the food more and that background noise mostly gets in the way of tasting by distracting people, with most studies measuring small rating changes in a lab. A 2011 lab study found loud background noise made food taste less sweet, less salty and crunchier, and a 2015 Cornell study of 48 people found airplane-cabin noise made sweet things taste less sweet and umami stronger, with no change for salty, sour or bitter; neither used music. A 2012 lab study found people described the same wine in line with the character of the music they heard, and a 2015 study at a real wine tasting with live classical musicians found the music changed how acidic and fruity the wines seemed. A 2022 study of 248 people at lunch in a Finnish cafeteria found meals lasted longer with any sound than in silence, and longer with slow music than fast, without people eating more, and liking the sound went along with liking the food. For a dinner, we'd suggest music the guests are likely to enjoy, at a level they can talk across, from a duo or a solo musician.
- [Party music for all ages](https://signetartists.com/blog/party-music-for-all-ages/): A research summary from a Denver live-music booking company on choosing music for a party with several generations in it. A 2020 study of 470 people aged 18 to 82 found that the songs bringing back the most memories came from each person's teens, peaking around age 14 inside a span of roughly ages 10 to 30, and a 2025 study of 1,891 people put the peak for personally meaningful songs at 17. An older 1989 finding of a peak at about 23 or 24 was not repeated in three later attempts. A 2013 Cornell study of 62 college students found a second peak for the music of their parents' youth, a 2015 German study of 48 older adults found songs from across five decades of their lives still brought back memories, and a 2024 study of 582 American adults found nostalgic songs felt more positive and energizing than songs that were only familiar. The post includes a table, worked out by the company from the 2020 and 2025 studies, of the years each guest age was 10 to 30 as of 2026, and closes with how a live act can move across the decades.
- [Live music for memory care residents](https://signetartists.com/blog/live-music-for-memory-care-residents/): This is a summary of what research shows about live music for people living with dementia, from a Denver company that books musicians for senior living communities. Two small studies (2006 and 2004) found residents more engaged during live music than during recorded music, and a 2012 Dutch study found caregivers and family reported better contact and mood after close-up performances by professional singers. A 2020 review of 15 studies credited recorded-music programs with the more consistent improvements in behavior and live music with better communication and relationships. The 2025 Cochrane review (30 trials, 1,720 people) found therapeutic music programs probably reduce symptoms of depression slightly, with no effect on agitation or aggression and nothing lasting four weeks after the sessions ended, and a 2022 trial of personal playlists in 54 nursing homes found no significant reduction in agitation or medication use. Songs released when a listener was about 10 to 30 feel most personal. The post also covers hearing loss, residents who come to dislike sound, the lack of any study on volume or time of day, and how a live performance differs from music therapy.
- [Is live music better than recorded?](https://signetartists.com/blog/is-live-music-better-than-recorded/): A research summary from Signet Artists, a Denver live music booking company, on whether live music is better than recorded music. It covers a 2019 motion-capture study in which an audience moved their heads faster at a live show than another audience did at a playback of the same album, a 2016 study in which listeners' heart rates followed the tempo only when pianists played live, a 2023 string quartet study in which people in the hall felt more connected to the rest of the audience than people watching a livestream, a 2023 study of audience heart rates and breathing at three chamber concerts, a 2012 meta-analysis on seeing performers, and a 2024 brain-scan study. It also covers what live music has not been shown to do, including the unsupported claim that going to gigs adds nine years to your life, and notes that no study has compared live and recorded music at a wedding or a party. Each finding is given with its size, who was studied and its main limitation.
- [How to get people to dance at a wedding](https://signetartists.com/blog/how-to-get-people-to-dance-at-a-wedding/): A research summary from a Denver live-music booking company on what gets people dancing at a wedding or a party. It covers a 2016 study of 46 dancers at a London club, where the crowd moved most in time with each other on better-known songs and at beats near walking pace (100 to 150 beats per minute); a 2018 lab listening study that put the drum patterns people most wanted to move to at around 100 to 120 beats per minute; a 2005 study that found people move at a steady 2 steps a second; a 2022 concert at McMaster University where bass too low to hear made the audience move about 12% more; a 2019 study where heads moved faster at a live show than at a playback of the same album; a 2012 count of singing along across 30 nights in the north of England; and 2011 brain-imaging research on dopamine and anticipation. Each finding is given with its limits. It ends with what the company has seen work for placing the dance floor, which is experience rather than research, and what its bands and DJs do.
- [How does music affect people at a party?](https://signetartists.com/blog/how-does-music-affect-people-at-a-party/): This is the front page of a research series from Signet Artists, a Denver live music booking company, on how music affects people's behavior at parties and events. It summarizes what studies have found about volume and conversation, dancing, the music of different age groups, live versus recorded music, drinking, live music in memory care and sound baths, with a link to a fuller post on each. It lists popular claims that didn't hold up when checked against the research, including that people's favorite music comes from age 23, that going to gigs adds nine years to your life, that music reduces agitation in dementia, that slow music makes diners spend more, and that making music together makes children kinder. It explains the method used across the series: for every claim, what was found, how big the effect was, who was studied and the main limitation.
- [Does loud music make people drink more?](https://signetartists.com/blog/does-loud-music-make-people-drink-more/): A research summary from Signet Artists, a Denver live music booking company, on whether loud music makes people drink more. It covers the 2008 French study of 40 men in two bars behind the claim and why its evidence is in question (the same group's 2004 bar study carries an expression of concern, the lead author has had other papers retracted, and no other group has repeated the experiment in a bar), a 2013 lab study in which women finished a drink faster with music than in silence whatever the tempo, a 2012 lab study in which music made drinks taste sweeter, a study of 60 European bars in which loudness stopped predicting intoxication once other factors were accounted for, and acoustics research on the sound levels at which guests can still talk. It ends with practical guidance for the music at a company party: keep the talking part of the evening at a level people can talk across and let the dance floor be louder.
- [Do sound baths work?](https://signetartists.com/blog/do-sound-baths-work/): A summary of the research on sound baths from Signet Artists, a Denver booking company whose roster includes a sound bath. A 2017 observational study of 62 adults with no control group found less tension, anger, fatigue and low mood after sound meditations of about an hour on singing bowls, gongs and bells. A 2023 randomized trial of 50 anxious adults found that one session of singing bowls and one session of muscle relaxation both lowered anxiety compared with a waiting list, the bowls a little more, with about 17 people per group. A 2020 study of 48 adults found people felt slightly less sleepy after a struck bowl while a pupil measure of sleepiness showed no difference. A 2020 review found four studies and could not recommend singing bowl therapies; a 2025 review of 19 studies of mixed quality said they may have potential for anxiety, low mood and sleep. We found no study showing that a sound bath treats any condition. What a sound bath offers is an hour or so of rest, and people often say they feel calmer afterward.

## Acts

All acts and configurations are subject to availability.

- Tejas Singh (Singer-songwriter covers, fronted by Tejas Singh): Authentic and intimate with a specialty in building familiar songs from the ground up with his amazing ear and looping tech, Tejas brings a wide variety of fan favorite songs and is also available to play his original, singer-songwriter material to your event. Configurations: Duo to quartet. https://signetartists.com/artists/tejas-singh/
- Jazz Duo (Jazz standards, Upright bass and guitar): Class it up with jazz standards on upright bass and guitar, bring immediate sophistication to any cocktail hour or special event. The Signet Jazz duo specializes in music for when guests arrive, sip cocktails or enjoy dinner. This act is the perfect musical glue that holds the night together effortlessly. The volume and genre sit perfectly under riveting conversations. Configurations: Duo to trio. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/jazz-duo-trio/
- Dirty Flamenco (Flamenco, fronted by Gary Meyers): Brilliant, guitar-based flamenco musical act and one of the only in Colorado available for private events. Dirty flamenco plays real palos, and rhumba both authentically and with a soulful twist. Their polish as a working group is matched by their extensive standing repertoire. Configurations: Trio, larger by request. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/flamenco-trio/
- Funk Band (Funk and soul, Guitar, bass and drums, with a horn or keys at quartet size): This band plays instrumental funk and soul covers, and it's a great pick for a party where the dance floor is right next to the tables. You can book it as a trio of guitar, bass and drums, or add a horn or keys for a quartet if you'd like a bigger sound. Configurations: Trio to quartet. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/funk-band/
- DJ (All kinds of music (open format), A DJ and a sound system sized to your venue): Book a DJ on their own or to carry a late night set after the band wraps their set. All run by the same team, with the same contract. A solid DJ gets people moving and is the most common single booking of the corporate season. Configurations: solo to duo. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/dj/
- Tony Medina (Blues, rock and roots, fronted by Tony Medina): Tony Medina has a smoky voice, and he plays guitar with all the rhythm of a funk player. He plays the blues and the rock and roll that came out of it, from Freddie King and B.B. King to The Cars and Prince, along with his own songs. He can play solo for welcome drinks and dinner, or bring a four piece when you want people dancing. Configurations: Solo to quartet. https://signetartists.com/artists/tony-medina/
- Little Moses Jones (90s and 2000s R&B and hip-hop, fronted by Little Moses Jones): If your crowd grew up on Usher, TLC, Outkast, Missy Elliott, Lauryn Hill and Warren G, Little Moses Jones is the band to book. It's a six-piece band, and they rap the verses live. The band brings its own sound engineer, so you usually won't need a separate audio company, and they can keep the lyrics clean when you need that. It's a great choice for holiday parties, galas, weddings and milestone birthdays. Configurations: Six piece, with its own sound engineer. https://signetartists.com/artists/little-moses-jones/
- Meghan Clarisse (Country and Americana, fronted by Meghan Clarisse): Meghan Clarisse is a Denver singer-songwriter who calls what she does "music with country roots and cowgirl boots." Her latest album won the 2026 Josie Music Award for Folk/Americana Album of the Year, and she plays Dolly Parton, Fleetwood Mac and Johnny Cash alongside her own songs. You can book her solo, as a duo or with her five-piece band. Configurations: Solo, duo or five-piece band. https://signetartists.com/artists/meghan-clarisse/
- Quadrasonic (Alternative rock covers, Lead vocals, electric guitar, bass and drums): Quadrasonic is a hard-hitting alternative rock band from the Vail Valley. They play the rock songs everyone knows from Pat Benatar, Blondie, No Doubt, Nirvana, The Cranberries and Paramore, with a powerhouse singer out front, and they're an excellent choice for a wedding reception or a party where you want people dancing. Configurations: Four-piece band. https://signetartists.com/artists/quadrasonic/
- Chelsey Webb (Country, rock and pop, fronted by Chelsey Webb): Chelsey Webb is a Denver country singer raised in Alabama, and she was named Female Entertainer of the Year at the 2025 Colorado Country Music Hall of Fame awards. She plays country, rock and pop covers alongside her own songs, as a duo with her husband or with her five or six-piece band, and her band is an excellent choice when you want people dancing. Configurations: Duo or full band. https://signetartists.com/artists/chelsey-webb/
- Afro House DJ (Afro house, deep house, amapiano, techno and electronic, One DJ, plus live tabla hand drums on request): A great house track gets people out onto the dance floor, and live drums over the top of it can keep them there. This Denver DJ plays Afro house, deep house, amapiano (a style of house music built around piano), techno and electronic music, and can play the tabla over the set, so you get a DJ and a live drummer in one person. It's a great booking for after-parties, holiday parties, weddings and birthdays across Colorado. Configurations: DJ. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/afro-house-dj/
- Last Consulate (Instrumental downtempo, Upright bass, guitar and electronics, one musician): One player, upright bass and guitar out front, over downtempo electronics with slow hip-hop drums, worn keys and delayed guitar. Jazz improvisation on top, at conversation volume. Arrival, cocktails and dinner, on original material that sounds closer to an early-2000s downtempo record than to a jazz set. Configurations: Solo. https://signetartists.com/artists/last-consulate/
- Live Band Karaoke (Party covers from the 80s and 90s onward, Voice and guitar, keys, bass, drums, and a host working the mic): This party band plays 80s and 90s hits on its own, then hands the mic to anyone in the crowd who wants a turn. The words are up on a screen, and the band follows whoever's singing. Configurations: Quartet to six piece. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/live-band-karaoke/
- Yacht Rock Band (Yacht rock, Three voices, keys, guitar, bass, drums and saxophone): This band plays the Doobie Brothers, Steely Dan, Hall and Oates, Toto and Christopher Cross, with three voices in harmony and the saxophone out front. It's an excellent choice for a summer party, and most of your guests will know the words. Configurations: Quartet to six piece. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/yacht-rock/
- Americana Band (Americana and Colorado favorites, Voice and acoustic guitar, fiddle or mandolin, upright bass, drums): If your guests are flying in and you want your event to sound like Colorado, this is a great band to book. The band plays the Grateful Dead, Tom Petty and Neil Young alongside Nathaniel Rateliff and Gregory Alan Isakov, and it's an easy choice for a welcome reception, a ranch dinner or a summer picnic. Configurations: Trio to quartet. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/americana-band/
- Soul and R&B Band (Soul and R&B, Voice, keys, guitar, bass, drums, and a horn if you'd like one): A singer out front leads the band through Stevie Wonder, Aretha Franklin, Al Green, Bill Withers and the Motown songbook, and if you'd like a horn on the big choruses, we can add one. Bring this band in when you want people dancing at a holiday party or a gala. Configurations: Quartet to six piece. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/soul-band/
- Solo Piano (Cocktail piano, Piano, with a singer if you'd like one): A pianist can play from the time your guests arrive through cocktails and dinner, with standards and covers at a level they can easily talk over. It's a great choice for a hotel ballroom or a client dinner, and we can add a singer if you'd like. Configurations: Solo. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/solo-piano/
- Changes Jazz Trio (Modern jazz, Doug Emery on guitar, Sri Viswanath on bass and Brian Jaffe on drums): With the right jazz trio, your cocktail hour can feel like a night out at a great little club. Changes plays jazz standards with a modern edge on guitar, bass and drums, and the trio can keep the volume low enough for your guests to talk. They're all Denver musicians, and we can add a saxophone if you'd like the music to take center stage for a while. Configurations: Trio to quartet. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/changes-jazz-trio/
- Firstwater (Sound bath and sound healing, one facilitator, live instruments and a sound system tuned to the venue): A sound bath for your team, offsite or retreat. Your people lie down in low light for seventy-five minutes with nothing to do and nothing to say, with live instruments played over composed music and bass deep enough to feel in your chest, and Firstwater opens and closes the session with ceremony. Firstwater brings it to your venue or holds it in a partner space in Denver, and it books for wellness weeks, team building days, retreats and transition days. Configurations: One facilitator, seventy-five minutes. https://signetartists.com/artists/firstwater/
- René Moffatt (Original singer-songwriter, fronted by René Moffatt): It's a special thing to hear a song from the person who wrote it, and that's what you get with René Moffatt. He sings his own songs with an acoustic guitar. His music is folk and Americana, and it fits right in on a playlist with Josh Ritter and The Avett Brothers. You can book him on his own, or he can bring his band, René Moffatt & The Moonshadows, if you'd like a bigger sound. Configurations: Solo to quartet. https://signetartists.com/artists/rene-moffatt/
- Your Bird Can Sing (Beatles songs, and everybody sings, a Beatles sing-along led by two musicians, for everyone from five to ninety): You know the part of Hey Jude where everyone starts singing. A Beatles sing-along is a playful hour of that. Two musicians play and lead the singing, and by the second song that's your whole crowd. It books for family parties, company events, weddings, community programs and senior living, indoors or out. Configurations: Duo. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/beatles-sing-along/
- Solo Guitarist (Blues, roots, jazz and Spanish flavors, One guitarist, with or without vocals): A solo guitarist is a great fit for a cocktail hour, a client dinner or a private dinner, playing blues, roots, jazz and Spanish flavors soft enough that your guests can keep talking. The guitarist can sing or keep it instrumental, and usually all we need is a small corner of your venue. Configurations: Solo. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/solo-guitarist/
- Singer and Guitarist (Acoustic covers with vocals, One voice and a guitar): A singer with a guitar plays the songs your guests know by heart, soft enough that they can keep talking. You can book just one hour or have music from arrival through dinner, and it's a lovely fit for welcome drinks, a cocktail hour, a dinner party at home or a small wedding. Configurations: Solo. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/singer-guitarist/
- Spanish Guitarist (Flamenco and Spanish guitar, solo, One Spanish guitarist on nylon strings): A Spanish guitarist can play rumbas, a Malagueña and familiar songs in the same style, all from one small corner of your venue. Book a Spanish guitarist for a wedding ceremony and cocktail hour, a dinner party, a milestone birthday or a corporate dinner. Configurations: Solo. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/spanish-guitarist/
- Acoustic Duo and Trio (Acoustic covers, Voice and guitar, guitar and upright bass, or all three): An acoustic duo plays the songs your guests already know, with voice and guitar or guitar and upright bass, and it can stay soft enough for everyone to keep talking. You can book it for just an hour or from the time guests arrive through dinner, and if you'd like a fuller sound, a third musician makes it a trio. Configurations: Duo to trio. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/acoustic-duo/
- Christmas Jazz Trio (Christmas jazz, Guitar, upright bass and drums with brushes): Most of your guests will know White Christmas and The Christmas Song within the first few notes. This trio plays the Christmas standards in a jazz style, along with a few jazz standards that have nothing to do with Christmas, and everyone can easily talk over it. You can book the trio for a cocktail hour, for drinks and dinner, or for your whole holiday party. Configurations: Solo to quartet. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/christmas-jazz-trio/
- Classical Strings (Solo violin to string quartet, Violin, viola and cello): The first notes of Canon in D begin, and every guest stands up and turns around. That's what a lot of couples are picturing when they ask for strings, and it sounds just as lovely at a cocktail hour, a gala, a long dinner or a memorial service. You can book one violinist, a duo, a trio or a full string quartet of two violins, viola and cello, and they can play music from Bach in the processional to Coldplay arranged for strings. Configurations: Solo to quartet. https://signetartists.com/ensembles/string-quartet/

## Pricing

Signet Artists publishes no price list, no starting prices and no hourly prices. Actual prices vary by date, size, hours and location. https://signetartists.com/pricing/ sets out what live music costs in the Colorado market, with each price attributed to the public source it came from, so a reader can set a budget before writing to Signet. To get the number for a specific night, send the date: https://signetartists.com/contact/

Travel beyond the Denver metro area, a night's lodging past the passes, holiday weekends and New Year's Eve are priced with the date.
